ui.docTitle: What actually keeps ADHD brains reading
ui.kicker: Research brief · ADHD and learning material · 30 Oct 2026
ui.title: What actually keeps {ADHD brains} reading
ui.lead: Fifty-six sources, boiled down to cards. Four worlds in any order, about 15 minutes. Each card says how strong its evidence is, because a lot of popular ADHD advice has none.
gist: **Why it's hard:** later rewards feel worth less (delay discounting, d = 0.43), boredom bites harder, and working memory holds less.
**What helps:** short sections with a payoff each, feedback that explains, low-stakes quiz questions, clear headings and summaries, and nothing decorative.
**Games:** points and badges as the engine have no evidence for ADHD reading. Streaks that show breaks backfire.
**Myths:** Bionic Reading, dyslexia fonts, fidget spinners and "dopamine hits" don't hold up.
**The catch:** no study has tested adults with ADHD reading documents. These are careful inferences.
ui.planQ: Quick plan, if you like: when will you play the first world?
ui.planThen: Plan: {when}, I open the first world I haven't finished. One world, 3–4 minutes. (That's an if-then plan: card 6 of "What helps" says why.)
ui.calmOn: Calm mode: no XP or confetti
ui.changeAny: You can change it any time.
ui.finaleText: You now know more about ADHD and learning design than most of the apps marketed for it. This deck itself follows the rules it teaches.
finaleNext: Every principle, graded by evidence, with its sources: [the evidence table](https://github.com/calindumitru/ludify/blob/main/docs/evidence.md).

worlds.title: Why it's hard
worlds.tease: What the research says is different, and what's a myth.
recap: **Later rewards feel worth less** with ADHD: delay discounting, d = 0.43, in adults as much as children.
Boredom and ADHD go together (r = 0.40), and working memory holds less at once.
Attention doesn't fade fast: the gap is there from minute one, so **shorten the wait for a payoff**, not the reading.

cards.h: With ADHD, a reward later is worth less now
cards.p: Across 25 comparisons and 3,913 people, people with ADHD discount delayed rewards more steeply. Adults (0.40) and children (0.47) don't differ.
cards.more: This is the most solid reason to put a small payoff at the end of every short section, instead of one big payoff at the end of the document.

cards.h: How strongly do boredom and ADHD go together?
cards.why: r = 0.40 across 18 studies and 22,365 people. Boredom isn't a character flaw here; it's a measured pattern.

cards.h: With ADHD, attention collapses after a few minutes of reading.
cards.why: False. Across 47 studies the attention gap is large overall, but it barely grows over time: it's there from the start. So the fix is a near payoff, not just shorter text.

cards.h: Working memory holds less at once
cards.p: Meta-analyses find clear working-memory deficits in ADHD. A long paragraph that needs you to hold five ideas before the point arrives costs more.
ul: Put the point first, then the detail.
Keep what you need on screen, not in your head.
cards.src: Kasper et al. 2012 · Alderson et al. 2013

cards.h: Do rewards work better for people with ADHD?
opts: Somewhat, and immediate ones are preferred, but the findings are mixed
No, rewards don't work for ADHD
cards.why: Reinforcement improves performance somewhat more in ADHD (22 studies, 1,181 children), and children with ADHD prefer immediate rewards. But physiologically they seem less sensitive, and results are inconsistent.

cards.h: Nobody has tested adults with ADHD reading documents
cards.p: No controlled study looked at adults with ADHD and a self-paced document or e-learning course. Everything in "What helps" combines ADHD findings (mostly from children) with learning-design research on everyone.
cards.more: So treat the advice as well-informed, not proven. The grades on each card say how far each step is from direct evidence.

worlds.title: What helps
worlds.tease: Seven design moves, each graded by its evidence.
recap: **Short sections, one idea each, and a payoff at the end of each one.**
**Feedback that explains why** beats points for finishing. Quiz questions with answers help memory.
Cut the decoration: interesting-but-irrelevant extras **hurt** learning (g = −0.33).

cards.h: Give a payoff every few minutes
cards.p: Because later rewards feel worth less, end each short section with something gained now: an answer, a number, a decision.
cards.more: Strong on the ADHD side; nobody has tested it on documents directly.

cards.h: Which one raises interest in the material later on?
opts: Positive feedback that tells you what you got right
cards.why: Informational positive feedback raised later interest (+0.33). Expected rewards for doing the task lowered it (around −0.28 to −0.40). Feedback beats bribes.

cards.h: Chunk it, label it, sum it up
ul: **Segments:** short parts, and the reader controls the pace.
**Signals:** headings, summaries, bold key terms (d = 0.38 in general research).
**One idea per segment**, matching the working-memory finding.
cards.src: Rey et al. 2019 · Richter et al. 2016 · Alpizar et al. 2020

cards.h: Fun but off-topic extras ("seductive details"): what do they do to learning?
cards.why: They hurt: g = −0.33. Funny asides, decorative images and side stories pull attention from the point. Make the core itself engaging instead.

cards.h: Low-stakes quiz questions vs re-reading: how big is the memory boost?
cards.p: Effect size, g. 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.
cards.why: About g = 0.61–0.70 in general research: the testing effect. In small ADHD studies, students gained as much as everyone else.

cards.h: One if-then plan at the start
cards.p: "If it's after lunch, then I open section 2." Plans like this help (g = 0.31), and some analyses find them stronger in ADHD.
cards.more: Shown in children, including some with ADHD; not yet tested in adults with ADHD. The plan on this deck's first screen is one.

cards.h: Rank these by strength of evidence, strongest first
items: Easy stop and resume, with breaks
Points and badges as the engine
cards.why: Payoffs (strong ADHD basis) → quiz questions (moderate) → breaks (weak, no ADHD trial) → points and badges (no evidence for ADHD reading, and some harm).

worlds.title: Games and tools
worlds.tease: Does gamification work, and what's already out there?
recap: Games for ADHD move the trained task; real-life effects are small and shrink under blinding.
**Streaks that show breaks backfire.** Gamification novelty fades after about four weeks.
No tool converts a document into an ADHD-friendly version that keeps its interactive parts: that's a real gap.

cards.h: Gamified ADHD programmes: the best estimate
cards.p: Across 27 trials with 2,911 young people, gamified interventions improved symptoms a little, and only on parent- or child-rated scales. Corrected for missing studies: 0.17.
cards.more: A 2025 meta-analysis found no gains in working memory or inhibition. A 2025 review called effects beyond the game itself "unconvincing".
cards.src: Bryant et al. 2024 · Schultz et al. 2025

cards.h: EndeavorRx, the FDA-cleared ADHD game. What did its trial show?
opts: Better attention test scores, but no difference in rated symptoms
cards.why: Attention-test change 0.93 vs 0.03 (348 children), but rated symptoms didn't differ from the control game. The adult trial had no control group.

cards.h: Gamifying a course always boosts motivation.
cards.why: False. On average gamification helps learning (g = 0.49), but a 16-week gamified course **lowered** motivation and exam scores, and the novelty starts fading after about four weeks.

cards.h: An app shows you've broken your 12-day streak. What happens next, on average?
opts: People are less likely to keep going
cards.why: Seeing a broken streak makes people less likely to continue. That's why this deck has no streaks: leaving for a week costs you nothing.

cards.h: Which ADHD-marketed reading or focus tool has independent evidence that it helps?
cards.why: None. Bionic Reading's only positive result is its own 12-person pilot. Brain.fm's paper was co-written by its head of science. NotebookLM makes no ADHD claim.

cards.h: Google's "Learn Your Way" came closest
cards.p: It rebuilds a textbook chapter into levelled text, quizzes, narrated slides and a mind map. Recall after 3–5 days: **78% vs 67%** for the plain chapter.
cards.more: One chapter, 60 students, none selected for ADHD, run by Google. The gain came from several formats and recall quizzes, not from points or badges.

cards.h: Nothing converts a document like this one
cards.p: Generators such as NotebookLM turn text into audio, mind maps and quizzes, but drop the interactive parts and keep everything in their own app. Game builders need everything written by hand. ADHD-branded tools change how text looks, not how it's built.
cards.more: The W3C's cognitive-accessibility guidance (COGA) is the best checklist found: it names ADHD and covers page purpose, chunking and summaries.

worlds.title: Myth busters
worlds.tease: The boss level: popular ADHD advice, true or false?
recap: Bionic Reading, dyslexia fonts and colour overlays: no better than plain text.
Fidget spinners hurt attention; ordinary movement is a different thing.
"Dopamine hits" is a story; what holds is behavioural: **sooner, more frequent payoffs**.

cards.h: Bionic Reading (bold first letters) helps ADHD readers.
cards.why: Myth. Four controlled studies (2024–26) found no benefit and one found a cost. None tested ADHD readers specifically, and the vendor's own pilot had 12 people. Readwise's 1,916 readers: 325 vs 328 words a minute.

cards.h: ADHD is a dopamine shortage, so learning needs "dopamine hits".
cards.why: Myth, or at least a big overreach. It rests on one correlational brain-scan study of 53 people. What holds up is behavioural: sooner, more frequent payoffs matter more.
cards.src: Volkow et al. 2009 · Faraone et al. 2021

cards.h: Fidget spinners help children with ADHD focus.
cards.why: Myth. In 60 young children with ADHD, spinners made attention worse. General movement is different: boys with ADHD who moved more did better on working-memory tasks.
cards.src: Graziano et al. 2020 · Sarver et al. 2015

cards.h: Which of these have been proven in a trial with ADHD participants?
cards.why: If-then plans (in children, including ADHD) and retrieval practice (four small ADHD studies) have trials. Pomodoro and body doubling have **none** with ADHD participants, though both are low-risk to try.

cards.h: Dyslexia fonts and coloured overlays make reading easier.
cards.why: Myth. They perform no better than placebo in controlled tests.
cards.src: Kuster et al. 2018 · Griffiths et al. 2016

cards.h: A progress bar always keeps people going.
cards.why: Myth. Steady bars don't reduce drop-off, and bars that start slowly increase it. Showing what's left in plain units (like "12 cards left") is the safer bet; that's what this deck does at the top.

cards.h: Optional white or pink noise can help some people with ADHD.
cards.why: A small yes: g = 0.249 in ADHD, with small harm for people without ADHD. That's why it should only ever be an option, never the default.
